summary:
Kebbi lies within Nigeria, where same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA). Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that the Act reaches well beyond marriage, banning cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The penalties apply to any person present in the country, including visitors.

Entry carries criminal exposure. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

Kebbi is one of the twelve northern states that re-adopted criminal Sharia. Human Rights Watch (2004) records that Zamfara first re-adopted criminal Sharia with its Shari'a Establishment Law enacted 27 October 1999 and in force 27 January 2000, and that by 2002 twelve northern states, Kebbi among them, had Sharia criminal legislation and Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction over Muslims — the only states with such jurisdiction. Sharia jurisdiction in Kebbi therefore turns on the defendant's religion, while the federal SSMPA applies regardless.

Kebbi enacted its own Sharia penal layer in that wave. The Kebbi State Penal Code (Amendment) Law (Law No. 21 of 2000) was signed into law and came into operation on 1 December 2000, published in the Kebbi State Gazette Vol. 2 No. 1, Supplement, 31 December 2000. The enacted text states that whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm), and provides for lesbianism with up to 50 lashes and imprisonment of up to six months. The UK Home Office's June 2025 note carries Kebbi's own row in its twelve-state Sharia penalties table at section 8.4.3, confirming death by stoning for liwat (sodomy) and the 50-lash and six-month maximum for same-sex acts between women — the standard bloc penalty for women's conduct rather than the Kano or Katsina capital maximum. Kebbi's state code is thus broader in scope and harsher than the federal statute for Muslim defendants.

Ostien's annotated volume of northern Nigerian Sharia legislation lists Kebbi's Law No. 21 of 2000 and records Kebbi as one of three states, with Kaduna and Katsina, whose enacted text specifies stoning to death for sodomy.

Gender expression remains exposed, though no Kebbi-specific cross-dressing provision is sourced here. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available. Where such provisions exist they are state-level: secondary reference material records prison or a fine for men who dress or behave as women in some states, and a Kano court's 2025 sentence of a TikToker to one year's imprisonment.

Violence risk against trans and gender-nonconforming people is documented nationally. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja, with police describing the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing; The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing, a direct risk for visitors using dating apps. Police extortion is also documented: TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police who was struck with a gun butt and released only after paying part of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded for looking gay.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation.
